summary: Explains which parts of DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) must be implemented for stateless DHCP, in which a node gets settings such as DNS server addresses without the server tracking per-client state. The node must already have its IPv6 addresses from another mechanism, typically stateless autoconfiguration. It was replaced by RFC 8415.

eli5.summary: A computer already picked its own address. It just asks the network for extra info, like where the name lookup helper is, and the network does not need to remember it.

questions: how to get dns server in ipv6 without dhcp addresses
subtitle: Getting DNS and other settings in IPv6 without the server tracking per-client state.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes can pick their own addresses via stateless autoconfiguration, but they still need to know the DNS server addresses and other network settings. Traditional DHCP requires the server to track state for each client, adding complexity.
tldr.mechanism: Stateless DHCP lets nodes send a single Information-request message asking for configuration parameters like DNS servers. The server responds with a Reply containing only configuration information, without tracking anything about the client.
tldr.outcome: Networks can hand out DNS and other configuration settings without the server burden of maintaining per-client state. It was later obsoleted by RFC 8415.

today: RFC 3736 was obsoleted by RFC 8415, which is the current DHCPv6 specification. RFC 8415 provides a unified, consolidated specification for both stateless and stateful DHCPv6, replacing earlier RFCs including RFC 3315 and RFC 3736. Most modern IPv6 implementations now reference RFC 8415.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3736 defines stateless DHCP service for IPv6, a mode of DHCP where a server provides configuration information (such as DNS server addresses) to nodes without maintaining any dynamic state about individual clients. This is in contrast to stateful DHCP, where the server tracks address assignments and per-client lease information.

Stateless DHCP assumes that nodes have already obtained their own IPv6 addresses through a different mechanism, typically stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 2462). With their addresses already set, nodes then use stateless DHCP solely to retrieve configuration options needed for network operation.

This approach simplifies server implementation by eliminating the need for state storage and management, while still providing nodes with essential information like DNS servers, domain search lists, and SIP servers. The specification explains which parts of the full DHCP specification (RFC 3315) are necessary to implement stateless DHCP service.
sections.eli5: A computer already knows its own address. It just needs to ask the network for helper addresses, like where the name lookup server is. The network answers without remembering anything.

sections.title: How Stateless DHCP Works
sections.content:
Stateless DHCP uses a simple two-message exchange. A client that needs configuration information sends a DHCP Information-request message to a server, including an Option Request option that lists which configuration parameters it wants (for example, the DNS Recursive Name Server option). The server receives this request and responds with a Reply message containing the requested configuration parameters, such as a list of DNS server addresses.

Optionally, a client may include a Client Identifier option in its Information-request to identify itself to the server. This allows the server to customize its response based on the client's identity, even in a stateless mode. The server administrator can then use this information to provide different settings to different classes of nodes.

Unlike stateful DHCP, the server does not send any address assignments, does not track when clients will refresh their settings, and maintains no per-client database. This stateless nature is why the server burden is so much lighter than with traditional DHCP.
sections.eli5: The client says what it needs. The server says here you go. The server forgets about it. No tracking, no expiration times, no state tables.

sections.title: Required Messages and Options
sections.content:
To implement stateless DHCP service, clients and servers need to support only a small subset of the DHCP specification. Clients and servers both implement the Information-request message (sent by clients to request configuration) and the Reply message (sent by servers to return configuration). Servers and relay agents additionally implement Relay-forward and Relay-reply messages to handle cases where clients cannot reach the server directly.

For options, clients and servers use the Option Request option (to specify which parameters the client wants), the Status Code option (to indicate success or problems), and the Server Identifier option (to identify which server is responding). Relay agents use Client message, Server message, and Interface-ID options when forwarding messages.

Configuration options passed by stateless DHCP include DNS Recursive Name Servers, DNS search list, and SIP Servers. Optional options include Preference (to rank multiple servers), Elapsed time (to track how long the client has been configuring), User Class and Vendor Class (to provide hints for server response customization), and Authentication (to secure the exchange).
sections.eli5: The client asks for what it needs, the server answers, and if there is a middleman (relay agent), it helps pass the messages. A few simple options carry DNS servers, domain names, and other settings.

sections.title: Coexistence with Stateful DHCP
sections.content:
Networks often run both stateless and stateful DHCP. Some nodes may use stateless address autoconfiguration and stateless DHCP for configuration only, while other nodes request full address assignment via stateful DHCP. A server can be configured to support only stateless DHCP, in which case it discards any stateful DHCP messages (like Solicit or Request for address assignment) and leaves the stateful work to other dedicated servers.

Relay agents handle both types of messages transparently, forwarding stateless Information-request messages to stateless servers and stateful messages to stateful servers. This separation allows organizations to run different server implementations optimized for their respective roles without interference.
sections.eli5: Some computers want just settings, others want the server to remember them and give them an address. The servers can split the work, and relay agents pass messages to whoever is listening for what.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless DHCP is a subset of the full DHCP service defined in RFC 3315, so it introduces no additional security risks beyond those in the main DHCP specification. However, an attacker can spoof DHCP replies to direct clients to malicious DNS servers, mount man-in-the-middle attacks, cause denial-of-service problems, or carry out other attacks using the configuration information (especially DNS). These risks are described in detail in the specifications for each configuration option.

To defend against these attacks, implementations can use authenticated DHCP, as described in RFC 3315 sections 21 and 22.11, which uses cryptographic signatures to verify that replies come from legitimate servers. This authentication mechanism is optional but strongly recommended in untrusted networks.
sections.eli5: If the network is mean, someone could lie about DNS servers and trick you. You can ask for a signature to prove the answer is real.
